title: The Radiators of the family house on Kessler Street
premise: When Sebastian Pemberton's estranged father dies, the bridge inspector returns to the family house on Kessler Street to settle the estate, cataloguing his grief the way he catalogs cracks in steel. There he meets Wren, a stranger at the funeral who calls the family by a name nobody uses — a name from his father's first life, before Sebastian existed. As Wren's memories collide with Sebastian's careful silences, the two discover his father kept a second inventory: letters never sent, addressed to everyone he failed. Saying goodbye properly means reading them aloud, together, before the house — and its radiators, still warm with old winters — is sold out from under them.
about_author: Noor Villalobos is a former building conservator who spent a decade documenting houses slated for demolition, interviewing the families who left them behind. Her fiction is known for finding enormous feeling in small domestic machinery — hinges, boilers, and the quiet rooms where people almost said what they meant.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. At his father's funeral, Sebastian measures his grief like structural fatigue, noting everything unsaid between them over thirty years. A woman named Wren approaches the casket and greets the family as 'the Aldouses' — a name no one recognizes. The beat: numbness cracked by a single foreign word.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. He moves into the shuttered Kessler Street house to prepare it for sale, making lists of repairs and resentments alike. His sister Margot wants everything boxed fast; he wants to understand why their father never spoke of his past. Beat: avoidance dressed up as diligence.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren, a hospice volunteer who sat with the father in his final months, reveals he called himself Aldous then — and that he spoke constantly about 'the children on Kessler Street' she'd never met. She arrives with a shoebox of his belongings. Beat: the dead man becomes a stranger.

chapters.title: Radiators Still Warm
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. Wren visits the house; the boiler, ancient and illegal, still runs. In the basement they find a locked tin box inside the radiator cabinet. Margot forbids opening it until probate clears. Beat: warmth as evidence that someone kept tending this place.

chapters.title: Margot Counts the Cost
chapters.summary: Margot's POV. Margot, who carried the caregiving burden Sebastian avoided, resents both the stranger and her brother's sudden sentimentality. She reveals she knew about the name years ago and chose silence too. Beat: anger as a form of inherited loneliness.

chapters.title: The Letters Never Sent
chapters.summary: Sebastian and Wren's alternating POV. They open the tin: dozens of unsent letters — to Sebastian, Margot, a woman named Ada Aldous, and one blank. Reading the first aloud transforms the kitchen into something like a séance. Beat: the dead man finally speaks, imperfectly.

chapters.title: Ada
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The letters trace the father's first marriage and the child he lost — Sebastian's half-brother, dead at nine, after which he renamed himself Pemberton and fled into silence. Wren recognizes the pattern: patients rewriting themselves at the end. Beat: pity replacing judgment.

chapters.title: Load-Bearing Walls
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. A letter names Sebastian directly, apologizing for teaching him silence instead of words. Sebastian realizes he has built his own marriage on the same expansion joints, measuring rather than speaking. He calls his wife and says one true thing out loud. Beat: the turning point — grief becomes instruction.

chapters.title: Reading Aloud
chapters.summary: All three siblings plus Wren, POV rotating. On the last night before closing, they read every letter aloud in the cold house, radiators off, finishing with the blank one — which Sebastian fills in, writing back to his father at last. Beat: climax; the family speaks across the divide simultaneously.

chapters.title: What the House Remembers
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV, months later. The house is sold; Wren stays in touch, an adopted thread of the found family. Sebastian keeps the radiator valve as a paperweight and writes letters now, sent ones. Final beat: belonging isn't a place you inherit but a practice you begin, out loud, before time runs out.
